extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and advisors in Brazilian patent law (patent attorneys/agents, judges, policymakers, in-house counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive chapter summarizing Brazil's patent law (LPI), INPI practice, prosecution requirements, patentability standards, rights and exceptions, ownership rules, terms, and judicial/administrative remedies. Intended as a reference for advising, prosecuting, litigating, and judging Brazilian patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial application)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is granted only if the novelty, inventive step and industrial application requirements are met (Article 8 of the LPI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty: invention not comprised by the state of the art (Article 11). Inventive step: not obvious to a person skilled in the art (Article 13). Industrial application: susceptible to use or production in any type of industry (Article 15). These three elements must be simultaneously satisfied for invention patents; utility models have analogous but distinct inventive-step rules (Article 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patent protection (invention patent, utility model, certificate of addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of patents: invention patents (20 years from filing) and utility models (15 years from filing). Certificate of addition may protect improvements accessory to an invention patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invention patents protect new technical solutions to a technical problem. Utility models protect three-dimensional objects with a new form or arrangement producing a functional improvement (Article 9). Certificate of addition: may be requested to protect an improvement lacking inventive step but within the same inventive concept (Article 76); it is accessory to the patent and expires with the patent (Article 77). Application for certificate of addition is rejected if subject matter does not present the same inventive concept (Article 76(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must be presented clearly in firm, uniform lines and in indelible ink, with as many drawings as necessary and numbered consecutively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part/element must contain numerical references described in the specifications and claims. For utility model applications drawings are essential because the claims are always associated with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification / sufficiency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application or certificate of addition must be sufficiently specified: containing all details necessary to allow a person skilled in the art to reproduce the object and, where appropriate, indicate the best way of execution (Article 24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications should identify the existing problem in the state of the art and the proposed solution, specify technical sector, clearly highlight novelty, technical effect (for inventions), advantages over the state of the art, and for utility models show functional improvement and conditions of better use. Applications must start with a concise title (not a brand), describe a single invention or a group of interrelated inventions forming a single inventive concept, list drawings, and include a 50–200 word abstract (max 25 lines) summarizing technical characteristics and uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drafting and scope of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims determine the extent of protection; they must be based on the specifications and clearly and precisely define the subject matter, avoiding expressions leading to uncertainties (Article 25 and Article 41).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may be independent (protect essential technical characteristics) or dependent (include features of previous claims). In invention claims, after the preamble the expression 'characterized by' must define essential technical features. Multiple independent claims are allowed if connected by the same inventive concept; claims of different categories (product/process/apparatus) should show interconnection when appropriate using linking phrases. For utility models the main independent claim must fully characterize the elements, positions and interconnections; dependent claims may describe optional complementary elements or variations that don't change unity or operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and prior disclosure (including inventor grace period)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention or utility model is new when it is not fully described by a single prior art document existing before the filing date (Article 11). Disclosures by the inventor within 12 months before filing are not considered prior art (Article 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure in any form anywhere in the world destroys novelty unless it is by the inventor (or authorized person) within 12 months prior to filing/priority date. INPI may require a statement and evidence concerning such disclosure; the inventor may indicate it at filing. Unionist priority under Paris Convention (12 months) also preserves novelty vis-à-vis earlier filings abroad (Article 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority rules (unionist priority and internal priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unionist priority (Paris Convention) allows a 12-month priority period from first filing abroad; internal priority within Brazil allows a later Brazil filing to claim priority from an earlier Brazil filing by the same applicant within one year (Article 17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority is admitted only for subject matter disclosed in the previous application; new matter is not covered. Both earlier and subsequent applications must contain complete technical content. A divisional application cannot serve as basis for claiming priority. Internal priority does not extend time limits for claiming unionist priority abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention presents an inventive step if it is not derived from the state of the art in a manner that is evident or obvious to a person skilled in the art (Article 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere combinations of known characteristics or application of routine knowledge are not inventive. For utility models the inventive-step threshold is different: ordinary or common derivation from prior art is not allowed, but predictable technical effects and simple combinations may be accepted provided the new form/layout yields a functional improvement (Article 14). If invention requires combination of multiple documents, the issue shifts to inventive step (i.e., whether the combination was obvious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial application definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention or utility model is susceptible to industrial application if it can be used or produced in any type of industry (Article 15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical usability test: the invention must be reproducible and useful in industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter (Article 18 and Article 10 lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject matters are explicitly not patentable: items contrary to morals/public security/health; substances/processes resulting from transformation of the atomic nucleus; whole or part of living beings (except certain transgenic microorganisms) (Article 18). Article 10 lists subject matter considered neither inventions nor utility models (discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, pure abstract conceptions, business methods, literary/architectural works, computer programs, presentation of information, game rules, surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic methods, natural living beings or biological material found in nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transgenic microorganisms that meet novelty, inventive step, and industrial application may be patentable; Article 18 defines 'transgenic microorganisms' specifically. Therapeutic/diagnostic/surgical methods for application to the human/animal body are excluded. Computer programs are expressly excluded under Article 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant and inventor identification; first-to-file presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The author of an invention is assured the right to obtain a patent; under the law the patent applicant is presumed to be entitled to obtain the patent unless proven otherwise (Article 6(1)). The right is guaranteed to the one who files first if two or more authors developed same invention independently (Article 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent may be applied for by the author, heirs, assignee, or person who holds rights under law or employment/agreement (Article 6(2)). Joint inventors may file together or one may file indicating and qualifying the others, as a disclaimer of their rights (Article 6(3)). Inventors may request nondisclosure of their name (Article 6(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights conferred by a patent and scope (products and processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent entitles its holder the right to prevent third parties from producing, using, offering for sale, selling or importing a product that is the object of the patent, and to prevent use of a process or products obtained directly by a patented process (Article 42).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The holder may also prevent third parties from contributing to the practice of these acts. If an alleged infringer cannot prove their product was obtained by a different manufacturing process, the process patent will be deemed infringed (Article 42(2)). Patent holders also have the right to obtain compensation for improper exploitation (Article 44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to patent rights (exhaustions and permitted uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holder may not prevent certain acts: private non-commercial acts; acts for experimental purposes; preparation of drugs per medical prescription for individual cases; acts performed with a product placed on the domestic market by the patent holder or with their consent; certain uses of patented living matter as initial source for variation/propagation without economic purpose; circulation/marketing of lawfully introduced patented living products provided not used to multiply; and acts to produce information/data to obtain a trade license in Brazil or other country after expiration of Article 40 time limits (Article 43 and Article 42 exceptions list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory exceptions carve out research, private use, pharmacist compounding, exhaustion by authorized market introduction, and regulatory trial activities. The list includes particular rules for living matter and downstream propagation/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of inventions developed in employment (ownership and compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions arising from an employment contract or resulting from services for which the employee was hired belong exclusively to the employer; compensation rules and ownership sharing are provided (Articles 88–93).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless otherwise agreed, compensation is limited to salary unless contract provides otherwise (Article 88(1)). If invention unrelated to employment and not arising from use of employer resources, it belongs to employee (Article 90). Where invention results from both personal contribution and employer resources, ownership is shared equally unless contract provides otherwise (Article 91). Employer must exploit the patent within one year of grant or ownership may transfer to employee (Article 91(3)). Rules extend to self-employed, trainees, contractors as appropriate (Article 92).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term, grant, and formalities (term, publication, letters patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention patents: 20 years from filing; utility models: 15 years from filing (Article 49). A patent is granted after application approval and proof of payment, with issuance of letters patent (Article 38).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment and proof must be made within 60 days of granting (Article 38(1)); patent deemed granted on date of publication (Article 38(3)). Letters patent must contain number, title, nature, inventor name, holder identification and address, term of validity, specifications, claims, drawings, and priority data (Article 39). Patents are territorial; valid only in countries granting protection (Article 4 bis of Paris Convention). Historical Article 40 provided minimum-term protections linked to INPI delay but was declared unconstitutional and later revoked; backlog and long prosecution times have practical term implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application filing channels and INPI administrative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications can be filed through INPI's 'e-Patentes' platform. INPI issues normative rulings, ordinances and additional administrative guidelines for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INPI is bound to the LPI, Paris Convention, TRIPS, PCT and has issued Normative Rulings No. 30 and 31 (2013) and other ordinances. INPI also houses training bodies and issues procedural guidance and resolutions that affect examination and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of attorney and representation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign applicants must appoint and maintain an attorney-in-fact in Brazil with powers to represent them in administrative and judicial proceedings, including to receive service of process (Article 217). Power of attorney must be in Portuguese and submitted within 60 days from the date of the first act of the party, under penalty of dismissal (Article 216).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consular authentication and notarization of signature is not required (Article 216(1)). Dismissal for failure to submit power of attorney is final (Article 216(2)). Any attorney regularly enrolled with the Brazilian Bar Association may act in the administrative stage; applications may also be filed without an attorney in certain cases but foreign applicants must appoint local counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence listing and biological deposit requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject matter contains nucleotide or amino acid sequences fundamental to the description, the applicant must present them in a sequence listing to enable assessment of sufficiency (Article 24). PR Resolution No. 81 (2013) sets procedures for electronic presentation of sequence listings. The Budapest Treaty is relevant for deposit of microorganisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence listings and deposits enable INPI to assess sufficiency of disclosure for biological inventions; follow INPI resolutions for format and electronic submission. Deposits of microorganisms may be recognized under the Budapest Treaty procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative nullity proceedings (grounds and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent's nullity will be declared administratively when any legal requirement has not been met; specifications and claims do not comply with Articles 24 and 25; subject matter extends beyond original application content; or essential formalities were not met during processing (Law No. 9,279, art. 50). Nullity proceedings may be filed at authority's initiative or by any person with legitimate interest within six months from grant (Article 51), and may also be filed at any time during the patent's term by INPI or any person with legitimate interest (Article 56).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative procedure: holder notified to provide a statement within 60 days (art. 52); INPI issues an opinion and notifies holder and claimant to provide statements within 60 days (art. 53). Note that Article 50's breadth has been criticized as potentially allowing nullity for formal noncompliances; Patent Law Treaty limits invalidation for certain formal defects in absence of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial nullity and infringement proceedings (jurisdiction and interplay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nullity actions are filed before the federal courts; INPI must intervene in judicial nullity actions if it is not the plaintiff (Article 57). There is an uncertain relation between patent nullity actions (federal courts) and infringement actions in which nullity is incidentally alleged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nullity is a declared issue for federal jurisdiction; coordination and cooperation between courts (CPC Articles 67–69) may be used to deal with procedural overlap. Judges must respect limits of matters raised by parties (CPC Art. 141).

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file rule and priority among independent inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more authors developed the same invention independently, the right to obtain the patent is guaranteed to the one who proves to have made the filing first, regardless of dates of invention or creation (Article 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal of a previous filing that had no effect gives priority to a subsequent filing (Article 29(2)). This elevates filing date over date of conception for entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims interpretation and process/product overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define and limit protection and are interpreted in view of specifications and drawings (Article 41). Process patents cover products obtained directly by a patented process; if possessor/owner cannot prove different process, process patent infringement is presumed (Article 42(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to clearly capture both product and process aspects where appropriate; ensure specs support any product-by-process or process claims to avoid invalidity or unenforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model drafting specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: For utility models, after 'characterized by' all elements constituting the model must be defined with their positions and interconnections. The set of arrangements and forms responsible for best use must be fully characterized in a single independent main claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility models may include complementary optional elements or variations in dependent claims that don't change unity/operation; a flat structured model may admit a dependent claim describing a secondary three-dimensional shape arising from flat structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exceptions for regulatory/experimental data (Article 43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts intended exclusively to produce information, data, and test results aiming at obtaining a trade license in Brazil or any other country for exploitation and sale of the product after expiration of time limits set in Article 40 are excepted (Article 43).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit carve-out protects regulatory trials and data-generation activities related to regulatory approval and is distinct from other experimental-use exceptions; consider timing and Article 40 historical context when assessing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/administrative time limits and prosecution delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical prosecution times at INPI have been long (average 11 years in 2015, in some tech areas 14 years); INPI efforts reduced average time to circa eight years. Historically Article 40 provided minimum term protections when INPI took long to grant patents, but its scope has been limited/declared unconstitutional and revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long pendency affects effective market exclusivity; practitioners should monitor INPI backlog, engagement plans to combat backlog, and legislative/judicial developments affecting term adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: INPI organizational role and normative instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: INPI is the federal autonomous agency responsible for patent granting, classifications, and implementing industrial property rules; it issues normative rulings, ordinances and resolutions that affect patent examination and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant instruments include Normative Rulings No. 30 and 31 (2013), PR Resolutions (e.g., 72 and 81), Ordinance No. 11 (2017), and other INPI guidance. INPI also provides courses and training which serve as key knowledge sources in Brazil.
